extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent practitioners preparing UK complete specifications (patent applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for preparing a complete patent specification in the UK: what to include, timing and procedural requirements, relation to any provisional specification, use of drawings, and principles of clarity, good faith, and sufficiency of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory contents of the complete specification
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The complete specification ... must particularly describe and ascertain the nature of the invention, and in what manner it is to be performed, and must be accompanied by drawings if required. It must commence with the title, and must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of instrument is Form C (Second Schedule, Patents Rules, 1890). Examiner will ascertain whether the nature of the invention has been fairly described and whether application, specification and drawings have been prepared in the prescribed manner and the title sufficiently indicates the subject-matter. If inadequate, the Comptroller may require amendments or refuse acceptance (subject to appeal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for leaving a complete specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If not left with the application, the complete specification may be left at any subsequent time within nine months from the date of application (Comptroller may extend time for payment of fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to leave the complete specification within due time will deem the application abandoned. Rule 50 requires applications for extension to state circumstances and grounds; Comptroller may require proof. There are fees for filing with application vs afterwards; acceptance and sealing deadlines (e.g. acceptance within 12 months has consequences) and limited further extensions under later Acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination, amendment and appeal procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner reports on whether the complete specification fairly describes the invention and is prepared in the prescribed manner; the Comptroller may require amendment before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner reports negatively, Comptroller can refuse acceptance until amended to his satisfaction; refusal is subject to appeal to the law officer who may hear applicant and Comptroller. Reports of examiners are confidential and not open to public inspection except by court order (sect. 9(5) as amended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between provisional and complete specifications (same invention requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete specification must describe substantially the same invention as the provisional; the nature of the invention must be the same though improvements and developments within the scope allowed by the provisional may be added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is permissible to narrow the provisional (e.g. provisional sets out a principle, complete claims a special mechanism) and to introduce improvements, mechanical equivalents, and developments 'within the ambit' of the provisional. But introducing a material addition or claiming something larger or different than disclosed in the provisional invalidates the patent (cases: Bailey v. Roberton, Edison phonograph case, etc.). The patentee cannot rely on the provisional to cure defects in the complete specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and role of drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings should accompany the specification where required (especially for machines); words and drawings are read together to explain each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings clarify relation of parts and should be used when verbal description would be unintelligible. Care must be taken not to bind the patentee to the particular form shown in drawings unless that was intended; where multiple forms are sought to be protected, the drawing should be shown as illustrative and the specification should state this. A patentee generally cannot rely on drawings to describe material parts not described in the letterpress (Clark v. Adie). Rules (Patents Rules) govern size and preparation of drawings and how provisional drawings may be adopted for the complete specification. Adding omitted drawings later has been allowed in exceptional cases but may be struck out if added improperly (Pullan's Patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith, openness and avoidance of ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor is bound to act with good faith: there must be no studied ambiguity or equivocal language, no attempt to keep anything secret; a full disclosure must be made; the statement must be fair, open, explicit, and honest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications with studied ambiguity or concealment will be vulnerable in court. The patentee must take the public into his confidence so the specification can be held good on its merits if disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definition of the invention and distinct claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must accurately define the invention so the reader may clearly understand of what it consists and must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed; vague formulations are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee should state 'My improvement consists in this...' or describe by reference to figures. A claim stating only 'I claim the improved machine substantially as described' is inadequate and may be colourable compliance only. Courts have invalidated patents where the specification did not indicate with reasonable clearness what novelty was claimed (Philpott v. Hanbury; Fairburn v. Household). Where a second patent for improvements is obtained, distinguish clearly the later improvements from earlier invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / sufficiency: must fully describe means of carrying invention into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must set forth how the invention is to be carried into effect so that the promised result may be accomplished; all necessary details, directions, and explanations must be correctly given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe all parts, apparatus, materials, ingredients; state proportions, quantities, times, temperatures etc. precisely if possible, approximately if necessary. Needful processes and operations must be fully communicated and clearly unfolded in proper order and perspicuous language. Omission of essential details (e.g. tempering medium, ingredient quantities, necessary apparatus) has led to patents being held invalid (Liardet v. Johnson; Rex v. Arkwright; Neilson v. Harford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to disclose subsequently discovered improvements or different modes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor, after lodging the provisional/specification but before lodging the complete specification, discovers an improvement or different practical mode of carrying the invention into effect, he is bound to give the public the benefit of that discovery in the complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complete specification may show discoveries made since lodging the provisional and additions to make the invention workable are permissible so long as the nature of the invention remains the same. Failure to include such improvements where previously described modes were disclosed can render the patent vulnerable (Woodward v. Sansum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title must correspond to the invention described
rubrics_metrics.description: If any part of the invention, as described in the complete specification, does not fall within the title, the patent may be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, a specification that expressly indicates applicability beyond the title (e.g. railway carriage doors applicable to doors of any carriage) may extend claims beyond narrow title wording. Care should be taken to ensure title and specification align.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot rely on provisional to cure complete specification defects
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee will not be allowed to read the provisional specification with the view of aiding or supplying defects in the complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complete specification must stand on its own as a fair and sufficient disclosure of the invention claimed; provisional may not be used to patch insufficiencies in the complete instrument (Macfarlane v. Price, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical errors: correction procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerical errors in a specification may be amended by order of the Master of the Rolls or by the Comptroller (in certain circumstances and on terms) after grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically amendments required court order (cases cited); under sect. 18 of the Act of 1883 such errors may be amended after the patent has been granted by the Comptroller on such terms as he thinks fit. Before issue, clerical errors in or in connection with the application may be corrected by the Comptroller under sect. 91.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and public inspection rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of examiners shall not be published or be open to public inspection, nor liable to production in legal proceedings except by court certification in interests of justice; specifications of abandoned or void applications are not to be open to public inspection or published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory protections limit disclosure of examiner reports and abandoned application materials. Accepted applications/specifications and drawings become open to public inspection after advertisement of acceptance (sect. 10; Rules 21 and 22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges between acceptance and sealing; limitation on enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: After acceptance of the complete specification and until sealing of a patent (or the expiration of time for sealing) the applicant shall have like privileges and rights as if the patent had been sealed on the date of acceptance, but an applicant is not entitled to institute proceedings for infringement unless and until a patent has been granted to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although acceptance gives some interim protections, the patentee cannot recover damages for infringements committed before publication of the complete specification (sect. 13) and cannot sue for infringement until the patent is sealed (sect. 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible scope of later elaboration and details
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inventor elaborates his invention and renders it specific in the complete specification he may give a fair development, including improved methods of carrying it into effect, provided nothing is introduced that cannot be brought within the meaning and purport of the provisional specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters of detail, even if not occurred to the inventor at the time of provisional filing, may be introduced if they give a better method of carrying out the invention or working it more easily (Lucas v. Miller). But a new departure or material addition beyond the provisional's scope is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish original and communicated (foreign) contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention is partly original and partly communicated from abroad, the respective parts should be distinguished in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not an adequate answer to say the patentee has stated all that was communicated to him; the specification must itself sufficiently describe the matter. If the foreign communication is sufficiently described, lack of disclosure of additional foreign inventor knowledge is not a valid objection (Plimpton v. Malcomson).
